records.source: וַֽיְהִי֙ בִּשְׁנַ֣ת שָׁלֹ֔שׁ לְהוֹשֵׁ֥עַ בֶּן־אֵלָ֖ה מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מָלַ֛ךְ חִזְקִיָּ֥ה בֶן־אָחָ֖ז מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה׃
records.gloss: And it was in [the] year three of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, reigned Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah.
pieces: In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah became king.

L.1: And it happened in [the] third year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel [that] Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah reigned.

R.1: Hezekiah son of Ahaz became king of Judah. It was the third year that Hoshea son of Elah had been king of Israel.

decisions.choice: reigned: began to reign, became king
decisions.reason: As in the accession formula throughout Kings (1 Kings 15:1, 9), the verb with a date marks the start of the reign.

decisions.choice: Hezekiah: a name meaning "Yahweh is my strength" or "Yahweh strengthens"
decisions.reason: The name is built from the verb "to be strong" and a short form of the divine name. Here it is spelled in its shorter form; verse 9 and much of the chapter use a longer form of the same name.

decisions.choice: the third year of Hoshea: the dates of Hezekiah's reign are hard to fit together
alternatives: Hezekiah's sole reign began about 715 BC
decisions.reason: This verse and verses 9-10 tie Hezekiah's first years to Hoshea's reign, so that Samaria falls (722 BC) in Hezekiah's sixth year. But verse 13 puts Sennacherib's invasion (701 BC) in Hezekiah's fourteenth year, which would make his reign begin about 715 BC. The numbers cannot all be counted from one starting point. One common answer is that Hezekiah first shared the throne with his father Ahaz, and that some dates count from that time; the text does not say which.

decisions.choice: two sentences, the date second
decisions.reason: Readable splits the formula into two sentences, as these books allow, and puts the new king first.

records.heading: Hezekiah king of Judah

records.source: בֶּן־עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ הָיָ֣ה בְמָלְכ֔וֹ וְעֶשְׂרִ֤ים וָתֵ֨שַׁע֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ אֲבִ֖י בַּת־זְכַרְיָֽה׃
records.gloss: A son of twenty and five year[s] he was when he reigned, and twenty and nine year[s] he reigned in Jerusalem; and [the] name of his mother [was] Abi daughter of Zechariah.
pieces: He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abi daughter of Zechariah.

L.2: He was a son of twenty-five years when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. And the name of his mother [was] Abi daughter of Zechariah.

R.2: He became king at the age of twenty-five, and he ruled for twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother was Abi, the daughter of Zechariah.

decisions.choice: a son of twenty-five years: twenty-five years old
decisions.reason: Hebrew gives a person's age as being "a son of" so many years (1 Kings 14:21).

decisions.choice: his mother: the queen mother named in the formula
decisions.reason: For each king of Judah the formula names his mother, who held a place of honor at court (1 Kings 15:13).

decisions.choice: Abi: a short form of the name Abijah
decisions.reason: 2 Chronicles 29:1 gives the name of Hezekiah's mother as Abijah daughter of Zechariah. Abi is most likely a shorter form of the same name, "my father is Yahweh".

decisions.choice: He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years
decisions.reason: The wording kept for the accession formula throughout Kings. Literal keeps the Hebrew "a son of twenty-five years".

records.source: וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה כְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֖ה דָּוִ֥ד אָבִֽיו׃
records.gloss: And he did the right in [the] eyes of Yahweh, according to all that had done David his father.
pieces: He did what was right in the sight of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, in every way as his ancestor David had done.

L.3: And he did the right in [the] eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, according to all that David his father had done.

R.3: He did what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said was right, in every way, just as his ancestor David had done.

decisions.choice: did what was right in Yahweh's eyes: the good verdict, without any reservation
decisions.reason: This is the good verdict of the regnal formula (1 Kings 15:11). Earlier good kings of Judah were praised but with a limit: they left the high places standing (1 Kings 15:14; 22:44; 2 Kings 12:4; 15:4). Hezekiah is compared with David "according to all" he did, and verse 4 shows that he removed the high places as well. Only Josiah is praised in such terms again (22:2).

decisions.choice: David his father: his ancestor David
decisions.reason: David lived some three hundred years before Hezekiah. "Father" also means a forefather, and Kings measures each king of Judah against David (1 Kings 15:3, 11).

decisions.choice: did the right in [the] eyes of / did what was right in the sight of / did what the LORD said was right
decisions.reason: The wording kept for the good verdict at each level throughout these books.

decisions.choice: his ancestor David
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "ancestor" for "father" wherever David is called the father of a later king, as 1 Kings 15:3 and 11 do; Literal keeps "father".

records.source: ה֣וּא׀הֵסִ֣יר אֶת־הַבָּמ֗וֹת וְשִׁבַּר֙ אֶת־הַמַּצֵּבֹ֔ת וְכָרַ֖ת אֶת־הָֽאֲשֵׁרָ֑ה וְכִתַּת֩ נְחַ֨שׁ הַנְּחֹ֜שֶׁת אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֣ה מֹשֶׁ֗ה כִּ֣י עַד־הַיָּמִ֤ים הָהֵ֨מָּה֙ הָי֤וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מְקַטְּרִ֣ים ל֔וֹ וַיִּקְרָא־ל֖וֹ נְחֻשְׁתָּֽן׃
records.gloss: He removed the high places and broke the standing stones and cut down the Asherah, and crushed [the] snake of the bronze which had made Moses, for until the days the those were [the] sons of Israel burning incense to it; and one called it Nehushtan.
pieces: He removed the high places, broke the standing stones and cut down the Asherah pole. He also smashed to pieces the bronze snake that Moses had made, for until that time the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} had been burning incense to it. It was called Nehushtan.

L.4: He removed the high places and broke the standing stones and cut down the Asherah pole, and he crushed to pieces the snake of bronze that Moses had made, for until those days the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel were burning incense to it; and one called it Nehushtan.

R.4: He removed the hilltop shrines, smashed the stone pillars and cut down the pole used to worship Asherah. He also broke into pieces the bronze snake that Moses had made, because up to that time the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} had been burning incense to it as an offering. It was called Nehushtan.

decisions.choice: he removed the high places: the first king of Judah to do so
decisions.reason: The high places were local shrines, often on hills, where sacrifices were made away from the temple. Kings counts it against even the good kings before Hezekiah that they left them standing (1 Kings 15:14; 2 Kings 12:4; 15:35). Deuteronomy 12:2-14 calls Israel to worship at the one place Yahweh would choose. The Assyrian officer later throws this reform back at Hezekiah (verse 22).

decisions.choice: standing stones and the Asherah: objects of Canaanite worship
decisions.reason: Standing stones were upright stones set up as sacred markers; the law ordered them broken down (Exodus 23:24; 34:13; Deuteronomy 7:5). The Asherah was a wooden pole or image standing for the goddess Asherah (1 Kings 14:23; 15:13). The word is singular here, "the Asherah": it may stand for all such poles in the land, or name one well-known pole.

decisions.choice: the bronze snake that Moses had made: the snake of Numbers 21:8-9
decisions.reason: In the wilderness Yahweh sent snakes among the people, and told Moses to make a snake and set it on a pole; whoever was bitten and looked at it lived (Numbers 21:8-9). Israel had kept it for some seven hundred years, and it had become an object of worship. Hezekiah destroyed it even though Moses had made it at Yahweh's command.

decisions.choice: Nehushtan: a name that plays on "bronze" and "snake"
alternatives: the bronze serpent (as a title of honor)
a piece of bronze (as a scornful name)
decisions.reason: The name sounds like both nechoshet, "bronze", and nachash, "snake", the same pair of words that Numbers 21:9 sets side by side. It may mean simply "the bronze thing", perhaps said with scorn: a lump of bronze, not a god.

decisions.choice: one called it Nehushtan: the name it was known by
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject and can mean "it was called": the name people used for the snake. It could also mean that Hezekiah called it Nehushtan, naming it with scorn as he broke it.

decisions.choice: hilltop shrines, stone pillars, the pole used to worship Asherah
decisions.reason: The wording kept for these words in these books. Literal and Balanced say "Asherah pole" for the singular "the Asherah".

decisions.choice: burning incense to it as an offering
decisions.reason: Readable adds "as an offering" to show that burning incense was an act of worship.

records.source: בַּיהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בָּטָ֑ח וְאַחֲרָ֞יו לֹא־הָיָ֣ה כָמֹ֗הוּ בְּכֹל֙ מַלְכֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה וַאֲשֶׁ֥ר הָי֖וּ לְפָנָֽיו׃
records.gloss: In Yahweh [the] God of Israel he trusted, and after him not was like him among all [the] kings of Judah, and [those] who were before him.
pieces: He trusted in {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel. Among all the kings of Judah there was no one like him, either after him or among those who were before him.

L.5: In {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} the God of Israel he trusted, and after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor [among those] who were before him.

R.5: Hezekiah trusted {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel. No king of Judah who came before him or after him was his equal.

decisions.choice: trusted: relied on Yahweh for safety
decisions.reason: The verb means to rely on someone for safety and help. It is the key word of this chapter: the Assyrian officer asks again and again what Hezekiah is trusting in (verses 19-22, 24, 30), and the answer is given here before he speaks. The words stand first in the Hebrew sentence for emphasis: Yahweh is the one he trusted.

decisions.choice: none like him: the highest praise, given for his trust
decisions.reason: The same kind of praise is given to Josiah, who had no equal in turning to Yahweh with all his heart according to the law of Moses (23:25). Each king is praised for his own mark: Hezekiah for his trust, Josiah for keeping the law.

decisions.choice: He trusted in the LORD ... Among all the kings of Judah there was no one like him
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the subject first and make two sentences. Readable says "before him or after him", the usual English order.

records.source: וַיִּדְבַּק֙ בַּֽיהוָ֔ה לֹא־סָ֖ר מֵאַֽחֲרָ֑יו וַיִּשְׁמֹר֙ מִצְוֺתָ֔יו אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־מֹשֶֽׁה׃
records.gloss: And he clung to Yahweh; not he turned aside from after him, and he kept his commandments which had commanded Yahweh Moses.
pieces: He held fast to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and did not turn away from following {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. He kept the commandments {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had given to Moses.

L.6: And he clung to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; he did not turn aside from after {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and he kept {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} commandments that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had commanded Moses.

R.6: He stayed loyal to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and never stopped following {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. He obeyed the commands {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had given to Moses.

decisions.choice: clung: held fast in loyal devotion
decisions.reason: The verb means to stick to or cling to, and is used of a husband holding to his wife (Genesis 2:24). Deuteronomy calls Israel to cling to Yahweh (Deuteronomy 10:20; 11:22; 13:5; 30:20), and Hezekiah does what it asks.

decisions.choice: his commandments that Yahweh commanded Moses: the law given at Sinai
decisions.reason: Hezekiah keeps the law that Israel broke. Verse 12 uses the same words, "all that Moses ... commanded", of the northern kingdom's failure.

decisions.choice: the commandments the LORD had given to Moses
decisions.reason: Balanced says "given" for the second "commanded", to avoid "commanded the commandments"; Literal keeps both.

decisions.choice: stayed loyal
decisions.reason: Readable says what clinging to Yahweh means: staying loyal to him.

records.source: וְהָיָ֤ה יְהוָה֙ עִמּ֔וֹ בְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־יֵצֵ֖א יַשְׂכִּ֑יל וַיִּמְרֹ֥ד בְּמֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֖וּר וְלֹ֥א עֲבָדֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And was Yahweh with him; in all that he went out he prospered. And he rebelled against [the] king of Assyria and not he served him.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} was with him, and he succeeded in everything he set out to do. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and would not serve him.

L.7: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was with him; in all that he went out [to do] he prospered. And he rebelled against the king of Assyria and did not serve him.

R.7: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} was with him, and he was successful in everything he did. He turned against the king of Assyria and refused to be under his rule.

decisions.choice: Yahweh was with him: Yahweh's help in all he did
decisions.reason: The same was said of Joseph (Genesis 39:2-3, 23) and of David (1 Samuel 18:14). Yahweh being "with" someone means his presence and help.

decisions.choice: in all that he went out he prospered: he succeeded in all he undertook
decisions.reason: To "go out" can mean to set out on any task, and especially to go out to war. The verb "prospered" means to act wisely and so succeed (Joshua 1:7-8; 1 Kings 2:3; 1 Samuel 18:14).

decisions.choice: rebelled: stopped paying tribute to Assyria
decisions.reason: Judah had been a vassal of Assyria since Ahaz paid tribute to Tiglath-pileser (16:7-8). Hezekiah stopped paying and refused to serve, most likely after the death of the Assyrian king Sargon in 705 BC. Sennacherib's invasion (verse 13) was his answer.

decisions.choice: refused to be under his rule
decisions.reason: Readable says what "did not serve him" meant: Hezekiah refused to be his subject king.

records.source: הֽוּא־הִכָּ֧ה אֶת־פְּלִשְׁתִּ֛ים עַד־עַזָּ֖ה וְאֶת־גְּבוּלֶ֑יהָ מִמִּגְדַּ֥ל נוֹצְרִ֖ים עַד־עִ֥יר מִבְצָֽר׃פ
records.gloss: He struck [the] Philistines as far as Gaza and its territories, from [a] tower of watchmen to [a] city fortified.
pieces: He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its territory, from watchtower to fortified city.

L.8: He struck the Philistines as far as Gaza and its territories, from watchmen's tower to fortified city.

R.8: He defeated the Philistines all the way to the city of Gaza and the land around it. He beat them everywhere, from the smallest lookout tower to the strongest walled city.

decisions.choice: the Philistines as far as Gaza: the coastal cities southwest of Judah
decisions.reason: Gaza was the southernmost of the Philistine cities. Under Ahaz the Philistines had taken towns in Judah's lowlands (2 Chronicles 28:18). Sennacherib's own records say that the people of the Philistine city Ekron handed their king Padi, who was loyal to Assyria, over to Hezekiah, which shows Hezekiah's power along the coast.

decisions.choice: from watchmen's tower to fortified city: everywhere, from the smallest outpost to the strongest town
decisions.reason: The phrase names the two ends of a range: a lonely watchtower in the fields and a walled city. It is used in the same way of Israel's high places in 17:9.

decisions.choice: He beat them everywhere, from the smallest lookout tower to the strongest walled city
decisions.reason: Readable adds "everywhere", "smallest" and "strongest" to show that the phrase covers every kind of place.

records.source: וַֽיְהִ֞י בַּשָּׁנָ֤ה הָֽרְבִיעִית֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ הִ֚יא הַשָּׁנָ֣ה הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔ית לְהוֹשֵׁ֥עַ בֶּן־אֵלָ֖ה מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל עָלָ֞ה שַׁלְמַנְאֶ֧סֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֛וּר עַל־שֹׁמְר֖וֹן וַיָּ֥צַר עָלֶֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And it was in the year the fourth of the king Hezekiah, it [was] the year the seventh of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria against Samaria and besieged it.
pieces: In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria marched against Samaria and laid siege to it.

L.9: And it happened in the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which [was] the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, [that] Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria and besieged it.

R.9: In the fourth year that Hezekiah was king, Shalmaneser, the king of Assyria, marched against Samaria and surrounded it with his army. That was the seventh year that Hoshea son of Elah was king of Israel.

decisions.choice: the fall of Samaria told again: 17:5-6
decisions.reason: Verses 9-12 retell, in nearly the same words, the end of the northern kingdom told in 17:5-6. Here the event is dated by Hezekiah's reign as well as Hoshea's, so that Judah's king stands beside Israel's end: Judah is spared for now, while Israel goes into exile.

decisions.choice: Shalmaneser: Shalmaneser V, king of Assyria 727-722 BC
decisions.reason: He was the son of Tiglath-pileser III. He began the siege of Samaria after Hoshea stopped paying tribute (17:3-4).

decisions.choice: the fourth year of King Hezekiah: on these dates see verse 1
decisions.reason: This date, with verse 10, places the siege of Samaria from about 725 to 722 BC in Hezekiah's fourth to sixth years. How it fits with verse 13 is discussed at verse 1.

decisions.choice: two sentences, Hoshea's date second
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the event in the first sentence and gives Hoshea's date after it. "Surrounded it with his army" for "besieged" follows 17:5.

records.heading: The fall of Samaria

records.source: וַֽיִּלְכְּדֻ֗הָ מִקְצֵה֙ שָׁלֹ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֔ים בִּשְׁנַת־שֵׁ֖שׁ לְחִזְקִיָּ֑ה הִ֣יא שְׁנַת־תֵּ֗שַׁע לְהוֹשֵׁ֨עַ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל נִלְכְּדָ֖ה שֹׁמְרֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And they captured it from [the] end of three years; in [the] year six of Hezekiah, it [was the] year nine of Hoshea king of Israel, was captured Samaria.
pieces: At the end of three years they captured it. Samaria was taken in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel.

L.10: And they captured it at the end of three years; in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which [was the] ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, Samaria was captured.

R.10: After three years the Assyrians captured the city. Samaria fell in the sixth year that Hezekiah was king. It was the ninth year that Hoshea was king of Israel.

decisions.choice: they captured it: the Assyrians
decisions.reason: The verb is plural, though verse 9 names one king. It speaks of the Assyrian army as a whole. Shalmaneser died about the time the city fell, and his successor Sargon II later claimed in his own records to have taken Samaria; the plural leaves that question open.

decisions.choice: at the end of three years: counted from the fourth year to the sixth
decisions.reason: Hebrew counts part of a year as a year, so the siege ran from Hezekiah's fourth year into his sixth, about 725 to 722 BC (17:5).

decisions.choice: the Assyrians
decisions.reason: Readable names who captured the city, which the plural verb implies.

records.source: וַיֶּ֧גֶל מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֛וּר אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אַשּׁ֑וּרָה וַיַּנְחֵ֞ם בַּחְלַ֧ח וּבְחָב֛וֹר נְהַ֥ר גּוֹזָ֖ן וְעָרֵ֥י מָדָֽי׃
records.gloss: And exiled [the] king of Assyria Israel to Assyria, and he led them in Halah and on Habor, [the] river of Gozan, and [the] cities of Media.
pieces: The king of Assyria carried the Israelites away into exile to Assyria. He led them away to live in Halah, on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.

L.11: And the king of Assyria exiled Israel to Assyria, and he led them [to live] in Halah and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and [in the] cities of the Medes,

R.11: The king of Assyria took the people of Israel away to Assyria as captives. He led them away to live in Halah, by the Habor River in the region of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.

decisions.choice: the parallel in 17:6: "settled" there, "led" here
decisions.reason: The verse repeats 17:6 almost word for word. Where 17:6 says the king "settled them" in these places, this verse has a verb that means "led them" or "guided them". The two words look alike in Hebrew, and the sense is close: the people were taken there to live. Every level keeps "led" here and words the rest of the verse as 17:6 does.

decisions.choice: Halah, the Habor, Gozan and the cities of the Medes: places in the far north and east of the Assyrian empire
decisions.reason: Halah lay in Assyria, northeast of Nineveh. The Habor is a river that flows into the Euphrates, and Gozan was a city on it. Media lay further east in the mountains of what is now Iran. Assyria moved conquered peoples far from home so they could not rebel (17:24; Isaiah 36:17).

decisions.choice: the Israelites (Balanced); the people of Israel ... as captives (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say that "Israel" here means its people, and Readable explains "exiled" as being taken away as captives, in the wording of 17:6.

records.source: עַ֣ל׀אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא־שָׁמְע֗וּ בְּקוֹל֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵיהֶ֔ם וַיַּעַבְרוּ֙ אֶת־בְּרִית֔וֹ אֵ֚ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר צִוָּ֔ה מֹשֶׁ֖ה עֶ֣בֶד יְהוָ֑ה וְלֹ֥א שָׁמְע֖וּ וְלֹ֥א עָשֽׂוּ׃פ
records.gloss: Because that not they listened to [the] voice of Yahweh their God, and they transgressed his covenant, all that had commanded Moses [the] servant of Yahweh; and not they listened and not they did.
pieces: This happened because they did not obey the voice of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God, but broke {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} covenant, everything Moses the servant of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had commanded. They would neither listen nor do it.

L.12: because they did not listen to the voice of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God, and they transgressed {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} covenant, all that Moses the slave of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had commanded; and they did not listen and did not do [it].

R.12: This happened because they did not obey {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God. They broke {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} covenant, everything that Moses, the servant of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, had commanded them. They would not listen, and they would not obey.

decisions.choice: did not listen to the voice of Yahweh: did not obey him
decisions.reason: To listen to someone's voice means to do what he says (Deuteronomy 28:15). The verse ends with the same verb: they did not listen and did not act.

decisions.choice: they broke his covenant: the reason for the exile
decisions.reason: The verse sums up the long explanation of 17:7-23. Israel's exile was not a mere defeat by a stronger power; it was the result the covenant had warned of (Deuteronomy 28:15, 36). The same words set Israel's failure against Hezekiah's faithfulness (verse 6).

decisions.choice: Moses the servant of Yahweh: the one who belonged to Yahweh and served him
decisions.reason: The word means a slave or servant, one who belongs to a master, not a hired worker. Used of Moses it is a title of honor: he belonged to Yahweh and spoke for him (Deuteronomy 34:5; Joshua 1:1).

decisions.choice: slave (Literal); servant (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As everywhere for "the servant of Yahweh", Literal says "slave" and Balanced and Readable "servant".

decisions.choice: This happened because
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sentence runs on from verse 11. Balanced and Readable start a new sentence and supply "This happened" so that the reason stands on its own.

records.source: וּבְאַרְבַּע֩ עֶשְׂרֵ֨ה שָׁנָ֜ה לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֗ה עָלָ֞ה סַנְחֵרִ֤יב מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ עַ֣ל כָּל־עָרֵ֧י יְהוּדָ֛ה הַבְּצֻר֖וֹת וַֽיִּתְפְּשֵֽׂם׃
records.gloss: And in four-teen year of the king Hezekiah came up Sennacherib king of Assyria against all [the] cities of Judah the fortified, and seized them.
pieces: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria marched against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.

L.13: And in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and seized them.

R.13: In the fourteenth year that Hezekiah was king, Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, attacked all the walled cities of Judah and captured them.

decisions.choice: the parallel account: Isaiah 36-39
decisions.reason: From here to 20:19 the story is told again in Isaiah 36-39, mostly in the same words. This verse matches Isaiah 36:1, except that Isaiah opens with "And it happened" and spells Hezekiah's name in its longer form. Verses 14-16, Hezekiah's payment to Sennacherib, have no parallel in Isaiah, which goes straight on to the officers' arrival at Jerusalem (verse 17; Isaiah 36:2).

decisions.choice: Sennacherib king of Assyria: his campaign against Judah in 701 BC
decisions.reason: Sennacherib ruled Assyria from 705 to 681 BC. After Hezekiah rebelled (verse 7), Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC. His own annals claim that he took forty-six of Hezekiah's walled towns and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage", and reliefs from his palace at Nineveh show the siege of Lachish (verses 14, 17). Jerusalem itself was not taken (19:32-36), so "all" means the walled towns of the land.

decisions.choice: the fourteenth year: dated from Hezekiah's accession
decisions.reason: If the campaign of 701 BC fell in Hezekiah's fourteenth year, his reign began about 715 BC; but verses 1 and 9-10 tie his early years to the last years of Samaria, before 722 BC. See the note at verse 1.

decisions.choice: walled cities
decisions.reason: Readable explains "fortified" as cities with walls, as in Isaiah 36:1.

records.heading: Sennacherib invades Judah

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח חִזְקִיָּ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֣ה אֶל־מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֩׀לָכִ֨ישָׁה׀לֵאמֹ֤ר׀חָטָ֨אתִי֙ שׁ֣וּב מֵֽעָלַ֔י אֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁר־תִּתֵּ֥ן עָלַ֖י אֶשָּׂ֑א וַיָּ֨שֶׂם מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֜וּר עַל־חִזְקִיָּ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֗ה שְׁלֹ֤שׁ מֵאוֹת֙ כִּכַּר־כֶּ֔סֶף וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֖ים כִּכַּ֥ר זָהָֽב׃
records.gloss: And sent Hezekiah king of Judah to [the] king of Assyria to Lachish, saying, I have sinned; turn back from on me; that which you put on me I will bear. And imposed [the] king of Assyria on Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.
pieces: Then Hezekiah king of Judah sent a message to Lachish, to the king of Assyria: "I have done wrong. Withdraw from me, and I will bear whatever you lay on me." The king of Assyria required Hezekiah king of Judah to pay {{units:about 11 tons of silver|300 talents of silver}} and {{units:about 2,250 pounds of gold|thirty talents of gold}}.

L.14: And Hezekiah king of Judah sent to the king of Assyria at Lachish, saying, "I have sinned; turn back from me. Whatever you put on me I will bear." And the king of Assyria imposed on Hezekiah king of Judah 300 talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.

R.14: So Hezekiah king of Judah sent a message to the king of Assyria at Lachish. He said, "I was wrong to turn against you. Take your army away from me, and I will pay whatever you ask." The king of Assyria ordered Hezekiah to pay {{units:about 11 tons of silver|300 talents of silver}} and {{units:about 2,250 pounds of gold|thirty talents of gold}}.

decisions.choice: verses 14-16: not in Isaiah
decisions.reason: Isaiah's account (Isaiah 36:1-2) passes over Hezekiah's surrender and payment and goes straight from the fall of Judah's towns to the officers' arrival at Jerusalem. Kings tells it, and so shows that paying did not stop the invasion: Sennacherib took the silver and gold and still sent his army against Jerusalem (verse 17).

decisions.choice: I have sinned: I have wronged you by breaking our treaty
decisions.reason: The verb means to miss the mark, to do wrong. Here a vassal king speaks to his overlord: Hezekiah admits that his rebellion (verse 7) broke his duty to Assyria. It is a confession of political wrong, not of sin against Yahweh.

decisions.choice: turn back from me: withdraw your army from my land
decisions.reason: The phrase "turn back from on me" asks the king to take away the weight of his army that lies on Judah.

decisions.choice: three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold: a huge tribute
decisions.reason: A talent was the largest weight, about 75 pounds. Sennacherib's own annals record that Hezekiah sent him thirty talents of gold and eight hundred talents of silver, with much else; the gold matches, and the silver may have been counted by a different standard or with other goods added.

decisions.choice: about 11 tons of silver; about 2,250 pounds of gold
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the weight in modern measures, with the talents as the alternative. Literal keeps the Hebrew units.

decisions.choice: I was wrong to turn against you
decisions.reason: Readable says what Hezekiah's wrong was: his rebellion against the Assyrian king (m2).

records.source: וַיִּתֵּן֙ חִזְקִיָּ֔ה אֶת־כָּל־הַכֶּ֖סֶף הַנִּמְצָ֣א בֵית־יְהוָ֑ה וּבְאֹצְר֖וֹת בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And gave Hezekiah all the silver found [in the] house of Yahweh and in [the] treasuries of [the] house of the king.
pieces: Hezekiah handed over to him all the silver to be found in {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s house and in the treasuries of the king's palace.

L.15: And Hezekiah gave all the silver that was found [in the] house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and in the treasuries of the house of the king.

R.15: Hezekiah gave him all the silver that could be found in {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s temple and in the storerooms of the palace.

decisions.choice: all the silver in the temple and the palace: the treasuries emptied to buy off an enemy
decisions.reason: Kings of Judah had done this before: Asa to buy help from Aram (1 Kings 15:18), Joash to turn away Hazael (12:19), and Ahaz to win Assyria's help (16:8). The king who trusted Yahweh (verse 5) now pays from Yahweh's own house.

decisions.choice: gave him
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "him", the king of Assyria, to whom the silver was given (verse 14).

decisions.choice: the LORD's house (Balanced); the LORD's temple, storerooms (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps "house"; Readable says "temple" for the house of Yahweh and "storerooms" for treasuries.

records.source: בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא קִצַּ֨ץ חִזְקִיָּ֜ה אֶת־דַּלְת֨וֹת הֵיכַ֤ל יְהוָה֙ וְאֶת־הָאֹ֣מְנ֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֣ר צִפָּ֔ה חִזְקִיָּ֖ה מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה וַֽיִּתְּנֵ֖ם לְמֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃פ
records.gloss: At the time the that stripped Hezekiah the doors of [the] temple of Yahweh and the doorposts which had overlaid Hezekiah king of Judah, and he gave them to [the] king of Assyria.
pieces: At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold from the doors of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s temple and from the doorposts that he, Hezekiah king of Judah, had covered with it, and gave it to the king of Assyria.

L.16: At that time Hezekiah stripped the doors of the temple of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and the doorposts that Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid, and he gave them to the king of Assyria.

R.16: At that time Hezekiah also stripped the gold from the doors and doorposts of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s temple. He himself had covered them with gold. He gave the gold to the king of Assyria.

decisions.choice: stripped ... overlaid: cut off the gold covering
decisions.reason: The first verb means to cut off or cut into pieces; the second, to overlay a surface with metal. Together they show what was taken: the gold plating on the doors, which Hezekiah cut away to make up the tribute of gold (verse 14). Solomon had overlaid the temple doors with gold (1 Kings 6:32, 35).

decisions.choice: doorposts: the supports of the doors
decisions.reason: The word is found only here. It comes from a root meaning firm or steady, and most likely names the posts or frames that held the doors.

decisions.choice: that Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid: he undid his own work
decisions.reason: The verse names Hezekiah twice: the gold he now strips off is gold he had put there himself, perhaps when he restored the temple at the start of his reign (2 Chronicles 29:3). The note is sad: the reforming king takes apart his own gift to Yahweh's house.

decisions.choice: the gold ... covered with it ... gave it
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the gold, which the verbs imply, so that it is clear what was given; Literal keeps "gave them".

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֡וּר אֶת־תַּרְתָּ֥ן וְאֶת־רַב־סָרִ֣יס׀וְאֶת־רַב־שָׁקֵ֨ה מִן־לָכִ֜ישׁ אֶל־הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ בְּחֵ֥יל כָּבֵ֖ד יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וַֽיַּעֲלוּ֙ וַיָּבֹ֣אוּ יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם וַיַּעֲל֣וּ וַיָּבֹ֗אוּ וַיַּֽעַמְדוּ֙ בִּתְעָלַת֙ הַבְּרֵכָ֣ה הָֽעֶלְיוֹנָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֕ר בִּמְסִלַּ֖ת שְׂדֵ֥ה כוֹבֵֽס׃
records.gloss: And sent [the] king of Assyria [the] Tartan and [the] Rab-saris and [the] Rabshakeh from Lachish to the king Hezekiah with an army heavy, Jerusalem; and they went up and came [to] Jerusalem; and they went up and came and stood at [the] conduit of the pool the upper, which [is] on [the] highway of [the] field of [the] washer.
pieces: Then the king of Assyria sent the commander-in-chief, the chief of the court officials and the chief officer from Lachish to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem, with a large army. They went up and came to Jerusalem. When they arrived, they took their stand by the water channel from the Upper Pool, which is on the road to the Fuller's Field.

L.17: And the king of Assyria sent the Tartan and the Rab-saris and the Rabshakeh from Lachish to King Hezekiah, with a heavy army, [to] Jerusalem. And they went up and came to Jerusalem; and they went up and came and stood at the conduit of the upper pool, which [is] on the highway to the Fuller's Field.

R.17: The king of Assyria was at the city of Lachish. From there he sent three of his highest officials to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem with a large army. They were the commander of his army, the head of his palace officials and the Assyrian commander. They marched up to Jerusalem. When they got there, they stood by the water channel that comes from the Upper Pool. It is on the road to the field where cloth is washed.

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:2
decisions.reason: Isaiah 36:2 has the king send only the Rabshakeh; Kings names three officers, the Tartan, the Rab-saris and the Rabshakeh, and so has plural verbs ("they went up ... they stood"). Kings also tells the arrival twice, "they went up and came", and adds "which is" before the road. The rest of the verse is the same.

decisions.choice: Tartan and Rab-saris: titles of high Assyrian officers, not names
decisions.reason: Both are titles borrowed from Assyrian. The Tartan was the highest officer under the king, the commander-in-chief of the army (Isaiah 20:1). The Rab-saris was the chief of the court officials; the second part of the title is the word used for eunuchs or court officials (Jeremiah 39:3 names a Babylonian Rab-saris).

decisions.choice: Rabshakeh: the title of a high Assyrian official, not a personal name
decisions.reason: The word is an Assyrian title, made of "chief" and an office usually taken to mean "cupbearer"; by this time it named one of the king's highest officers, able to lead troops and speak for the king. He is the one who speaks in verses 19-35. The text never gives his name.

decisions.choice: they went up and came, twice: the arrival told step by step
decisions.reason: The words "they went up and came" stand twice. The repetition slows the story as the army reaches the city. It may also have come about in copying, since some ancient Greek copies have the phrase only once; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: the conduit of the upper pool: the place where Isaiah met Ahaz
decisions.reason: The officers stand at the very spot named in Isaiah 7:3, where Isaiah met King Ahaz and urged him to trust Yahweh instead of seeking help; Ahaz turned to Assyria (16:7). Now Assyria's officers stand there to demand that Hezekiah surrender.

decisions.choice: the Tartan, the Rab-saris, the Rabshakeh
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the three Assyrian titles as titles, with the article, as the Hebrew has them and as Isaiah 36:2 keeps "the Rabshakeh".

decisions.choice: the commander-in-chief, the chief of the court officials, the chief officer
decisions.reason: Balanced translates the titles instead of keeping them as strange names. The Tartan is called "the commander-in-chief" as in Isaiah 20:1, and the Rabshakeh "the chief officer" as in Isaiah 36.

decisions.choice: the commander of his army, the head of his palace officials, the Assyrian commander
decisions.reason: Readable names the officers by what they did. It calls the Rabshakeh "the Assyrian commander", as Isaiah 36 does, because he is the one who leads the talks and speaks for the king.

decisions.choice: The king of Assyria was at the city of Lachish. From there he sent ...
decisions.reason: Readable says first where the king was, then sends the officers, to keep the sentences short, as in Isaiah 36:2.

records.heading: The Assyrian officers at Jerusalem

records.source: וַֽיִּקְרְאוּ֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֵּצֵ֧א אֲלֵהֶ֛ם אֶלְיָקִ֥ים בֶּן־חִלְקִיָּ֖הוּ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל־הַבָּ֑יִת וְשֶׁבְנָה֙ הַסֹּפֵ֔ר וְיוֹאָ֥ח בֶּן־אָסָ֖ף הַמַּזְכִּֽיר׃
records.gloss: And they called to the king, and went out to them Eliakim son of Hilkiah who [was] over the house, and Shebnah the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder.
pieces: They called for the king, and Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, went out to them, together with Shebna the secretary and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder.

L.18: And they called to the king, and Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who [was] over the house, went out to them, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder.

R.18: They called for the king to come out. Instead, three of Hezekiah's officials went out to meet them. They were Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the king's palace, Shebna, the royal secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, who kept the records.

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:3
decisions.reason: Kings adds that the Assyrians first called for the king, and has "to them" where Isaiah has "to him". Hezekiah does not go out himself; he sends three officials in his place. The rest is the same.

decisions.choice: Eliakim over the house, Shebna the secretary
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 22:15-25 Shebna was over the house, and Yahweh said that Eliakim son of Hilkiah would take his post. Here Eliakim holds that office and Shebna serves as secretary.

decisions.choice: secretary and recorder: senior royal officials
decisions.reason: The secretary handled the king's letters and records of state; the recorder (literally "one who causes to remember") kept official records and perhaps announced the king's decisions. Both offices appear among David's officials (2 Samuel 8:16-17).

decisions.choice: Shebna: one man, whose name is spelled two ways
decisions.reason: Here and in verse 26 the name ends in a different letter from verse 37 and Isaiah 36. The spelling differs, but it is the same man and the same name.

decisions.choice: Shebna
decisions.reason: Every level spells the name as in verse 37 and Isaiah 36, so that one man has one name.

decisions.choice: to come out. Instead, three of Hezekiah's officials ...
decisions.reason: Readable says that the Assyrians wanted the king himself to come out, and that his officials went in his place.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵהֶם֙ רַב־שָׁקֵ֔ה אִמְרוּ־נָ֖א אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ הַגָּדוֹל֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר מָ֧ה הַבִּטָּח֛וֹן הַזֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּטָֽחְתָּ׃
records.gloss: And said to them [the] Rabshakeh, say please to Hezekiah, thus says the king the great, [the] king of Assyria, what [is] the trust the this which you trust?
pieces: Then the chief officer said to them, "Tell Hezekiah, 'The great king, the king of Assyria, says this: What sort of confidence is this that you are trusting in?

L.19: And the Rabshakeh said to them, "Say, please, to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: What [is] this trust that you trust?

R.19: Then the Assyrian commander said to them, "Give Hezekiah this message: 'This is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: Why do you feel so safe?

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:4
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as Isaiah 36:4, word for word, apart from the spelling of Hezekiah's name.

decisions.choice: the great king: a title of the kings of Assyria
decisions.reason: Assyrian kings called themselves "the great king, king of the world", ruler over lesser kings. The officer never calls Hezekiah king (verses 19, 29).

decisions.choice: trust: the ground of Hezekiah's confidence
decisions.reason: The noun and the verb come from the same root as "he trusted" in verse 5, and the word runs through the speech (verses 20, 21, 22, 24, 30). The officer asks what Hezekiah relies on and mocks each answer: Egypt (verse 21), Yahweh (verse 22), Judah's own strength (verses 23-24). The reader already knows the answer from verse 5.

decisions.choice: the king's message runs to the end of verse 25
decisions.reason: The officer speaks as the king's messenger: verses 19-25 are the message he was sent to give, though in verse 23 he speaks of "my master" in his own voice.

decisions.choice: What sort of confidence is this that you are trusting in?
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps both the noun and the verb of trust, as the Hebrew does and as Isaiah 36:4 does.

decisions.choice: Why do you feel so safe?
decisions.reason: Readable puts the question about trust in plain words, as in Isaiah 36:4.

decisions.choice: the chief officer (Balanced); the Assyrian commander (Readable)
decisions.reason: The titles chosen in verse 17, used through the chapter.

records.source: אָמַ֨רְתָּ֙ אַךְ־דְּבַר־שְׂפָתַ֔יִם עֵצָ֥ה וּגְבוּרָ֖ה לַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה עַתָּה֙ עַל־מִ֣י בָטַ֔חְתָּ כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְתָּ בִּֽי׃
records.gloss: You have said, only a word of lips [is] counsel and strength for war. Now on whom do you rely that you have rebelled against me?
pieces: You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but those are nothing but empty words. Who is it you are leaning on, that you have rebelled against me?

L.20: You have said, "Counsel and might for war [are mine]," [but it is] only a word of lips. Now, on whom do you rely, that you have rebelled against me?

R.20: You say you have plans and power for war, but that is only empty talk. Who are you depending on that makes you turn against me?

decisions.choice: you have said: "I say" in Isaiah 36:5
decisions.reason: Here the king mocks Hezekiah's claim: "you say" you have a plan and strength for war, but it is only words. Isaiah 36:5 has "I say", one letter different in Hebrew, with nearly the same sense: Judah's preparations are mere talk. The rest of the verse is the same in both books.

decisions.choice: a word of lips: Hezekiah's claim is empty talk
alternatives: Do you think mere words are counsel and strength for war?
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets the words side by side: "you have said, only a word of lips, counsel and strength for war". It can be read as quoting Hezekiah's claim ("I have counsel and strength") and calling it empty, or as a question, "Do you think mere words are counsel and strength?" Either way the officer says Judah's plans have nothing behind them.

decisions.choice: a word of lips: empty talk, words with nothing behind them
decisions.reason: The same phrase is used in Proverbs 14:23: mere talk leads only to poverty.

decisions.choice: rebelled: Hezekiah stopped paying tribute to Assyria
decisions.reason: See verse 7. Hezekiah had since paid a heavy tribute (verse 14), but the officer still treats him as a rebel.

decisions.choice: You have said, "Counsel and might for war [are mine]," [but it is] only a word of lips.
decisions.reason: Literal sets out the claim first and the officer's comment after it, with brackets for the words the Hebrew leaves unsaid.

decisions.choice: You claim ... but those are nothing but empty words
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the wording of Isaiah 36:5 as far as they can, changing "I tell you" to "you claim" or "you say".

records.source: עַתָּ֡ה הִנֵּ֣ה בָטַ֣חְתָּ לְּךָ֡ עַל־מִשְׁעֶנֶת֩ הַקָּנֶ֨ה הָרָצ֤וּץ הַזֶּה֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִסָּמֵ֥ךְ אִישׁ֙ עָלָ֔יו וּבָ֥א בְכַפּ֖וֹ וּנְקָבָ֑הּ כֵּ֚ן פַּרְעֹ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְכָֽל־הַבֹּטְחִ֖ים עָלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: Now look, you rely for yourself on [the] staff of the reed the crushed the this, on Egypt, which leans a man on it and it goes into his palm and pierces it. So [is] Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who rely on him.
pieces: Now look, you are leaning on Egypt, this cracked reed you use for a staff. Anyone who puts weight on it will have it run into the hand and pierce it. That is what Pharaoh king of Egypt is to all who rely on him.

L.21: Now, look, you rely for yourself on the staff of this crushed reed, on Egypt, on which [if] a man leans, it will go into his palm and pierce it. So [is] Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who rely on him.

R.21: Now look! You are depending on Egypt to help you. But Egypt is like a walking stick made from a cracked reed. If you lean on it, it will split and stab into your hand. That is what Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is like for everyone who depends on him.

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:6
decisions.reason: Kings adds "now" at the start and "for yourself" after "you rely"; otherwise the verse is the same as Isaiah 36:6.

decisions.choice: the staff of this crushed reed: Egypt, a support that fails and wounds
decisions.reason: Reeds grew along the Nile. A cracked reed used as a walking stick gives way and its split end stabs the hand that leans on it. Ezekiel 29:6-7 uses the same picture of Egypt.

decisions.choice: Egypt and Pharaoh: Judah's hoped-for ally
decisions.reason: Egypt was then ruled by kings from Cush (19:9). Isaiah had warned Judah against looking to Egypt for help (Isaiah 30:1-7; 31:1-3); here the enemy says the same thing for his own reasons.

decisions.choice: depending on Egypt to help you
decisions.reason: Readable adds "to help you" and spells out that Egypt is like the cracked reed, as in Isaiah 36:6.

records.source: וְכִי־תֹאמְר֣וּן אֵלַ֔י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖ינוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲלוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣יו וְאֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔יו וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽיהוּדָה֙ וְלִיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִפְנֵי֙ הַמִּזְבֵּ֣חַ הַזֶּ֔ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֖וּ בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃
records.gloss: And if you will say to me, to Yahweh our God we trust, [is] not he [the one] whose removed Hezekiah his high places and his altars, and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, before the altar the this you will bow down in Jerusalem?
pieces: Or if you tell me, "Our trust is in {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} our God," did Hezekiah not get rid of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} high places and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} altars? Did he not tell Judah and Jerusalem, "It is before this altar in Jerusalem that you must bow down"?

L.22: And if you say to me, "In {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} our God we trust," [is] not {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} [the one] whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah has removed, and has said to Judah and to Jerusalem, "Before this altar you shall bow down in Jerusalem"?

R.22: Maybe you will tell me, "We are trusting {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} our God." But Hezekiah tore down {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s hilltop shrines and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} altars. He told the people of Judah and Jerusalem, "You must worship only at this one altar in Jerusalem."

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:7: "you all" and "in Jerusalem"
decisions.reason: Here the verb is plural, "if you all say", spoken to the officials and the people with them; Isaiah 36:7 has the singular, spoken to Hezekiah. Kings also ends the verse "in Jerusalem". Otherwise the verse is the same.

decisions.choice: Hezekiah removed the high places: his reform of worship
decisions.reason: Verse 4 told how Hezekiah removed the high places, local shrines on hills, and called the people to worship at the temple in Jerusalem, as Deuteronomy 12:5-14 commands. The officer treats this as an insult to Yahweh, as if Hezekiah had robbed his own God of worship.

decisions.choice: is not he the one: the officer misreads Hezekiah's faithfulness as unfaithfulness
decisions.reason: What the narrator counts as Hezekiah's greatest act of loyalty (verses 3-5), the Assyrian presents as a reason why Yahweh would not help him.

decisions.choice: did Hezekiah not get rid of his high places and his altars? Did he not tell ...
decisions.reason: Balanced turns the one long question into two shorter ones with Hezekiah as the subject, as in Isaiah 36:7.

decisions.choice: hilltop shrines ... only at this one altar in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable says "hilltop shrines", the word kept for high places in these books (verse 4), and spells out what "this altar" meant: the altar of the temple in Jerusalem, now the only place for sacrifice.

records.source: וְעַתָּה֙ הִתְעָ֣רֶב נָ֔א אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֖י אֶת־מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְאֶתְּנָ֤ה לְךָ֙ אַלְפַּ֣יִם סוּסִ֔ים אִם־תּוּכַ֕ל לָ֥תֶת לְךָ֖ רֹכְבִ֥ים עֲלֵיהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And now make a wager please with my master, with [the] king of Assyria, and let me give to you two thousand horses, if you are able to put for yourself riders on them.
pieces: Come, then, place a bet with my master the king of Assyria. I will hand you 2,000 horses, if you can supply men to ride them!

L.23: And now, make a wager, please, with my master, with the king of Assyria, and I will give you 2,000 horses, if you are able on your part to put riders on them.

R.23: Let me make a deal with you on behalf of my master, the king of Assyria. If you can find 2,000 men to ride them, I will give you 2,000 horses!

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:8
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as Isaiah 36:8, except that Kings repeats "with" before "the king of Assyria".

decisions.choice: make a wager: exchange pledges, take up a challenge
decisions.reason: The verb means to give a pledge or to enter into an agreement (Genesis 43:9). Here it is a mocking bet: Judah could not take up the offer.

decisions.choice: two thousand horses: a taunt about Judah's weakness
decisions.reason: Assyria's army was famous for its horsemen and chariots. The officer mocks Judah as too weak even to find two thousand trained riders.

decisions.choice: my master: the officer speaks in his own voice
decisions.reason: Inside the king's message (verses 19-25) the officer speaks of "my master", so the king's words and his own run together.

decisions.choice: two thousand men
decisions.reason: Readable repeats the number to make the taunt plain, as in Isaiah 36:8.

records.source: וְאֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖י הַקְּטַנִּ֑ים וַתִּבְטַ֤ח לְךָ֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְרֶ֖כֶב וּלְפָרָשִֽׁים׃
records.gloss: And how will you turn back the face of a governor, one of the servants of my master the least, and you trust for yourself on Egypt for chariotry and for horsemen?
pieces: Then how could you drive off a single governor, one of my master's lowest officials? Yet you put your trust in Egypt to send chariots and horsemen!

L.24: And how will you turn back the face of one governor [among] the least of my master's servants, and you rely on Egypt for chariots and for horsemen?

R.24: You could not even defeat one of my master's least important officers. So why do you trust Egypt to give you chariots and horsemen?

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:9
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as Isaiah 36:9, word for word.

decisions.choice: turn back the face: drive back, repel
decisions.reason: To turn back someone's face can mean to refuse a request (1 Kings 2:16), but here it means to make an enemy retreat.

decisions.choice: governor: an Assyrian provincial official
decisions.reason: The word, borrowed from Assyrian, names a governor of a province. Even one of the least of these officials, the officer says, is more than Judah can face.

decisions.choice: and you rely on Egypt: a mocking contrast
decisions.reason: The clause states the absurdity: Judah cannot face one minor official, yet hopes Egypt's chariots will save it.

decisions.choice: officials / officers
decisions.reason: The king's servants here are his officials, as elsewhere for court officials; Literal keeps "servants".

records.source: עַתָּה֙ הֲמִבַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הַמָּק֥וֹם הַזֶּ֖ה לְהַשְׁחִת֑וֹ יְהוָה֙ אָמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔י עֲלֵ֛ה עַל־הָאָ֥רֶץ הַזֹּ֖את וְהַשְׁחִיתָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: Now, [is it] without Yahweh [that] I have come up against the place the this to destroy it? Yahweh said to me, go up against the land the this and destroy it.
pieces: Now, was it apart from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that I came up against this place to ruin it? It was {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} who said to me, "Go up against this land and ruin it."'"

L.25: Now, [is it] apart from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [that] I have come up against this place to destroy it? {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'"

R.25: Do you think I came to destroy this place without the permission of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? It was {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} who told me, "Attack this land and destroy it!"'"

decisions.choice: this place: "this land" in Isaiah 36:10
decisions.reason: Isaiah 36:10 has "against this land" in both halves of the verse. Kings has "against this place" in the first, which may point to Jerusalem itself, or even to the temple, which Kings often calls "this place" (1 Kings 8:29-30).

decisions.choice: Yahweh said to me: the king claims Yahweh's backing
decisions.reason: The claim is the Assyrian's, meant to shake Judah's trust. It holds a twisted truth: in Isaiah 10:5-15 Yahweh calls Assyria the rod of his anger against his people, but condemns the king who boasts as if he acted by his own strength. Yahweh's answer comes in 19:21-28.

decisions.choice: destroy: ruin, lay waste
decisions.reason: The verb is used for ruining a land or a city in war (Genesis 19:13).

decisions.choice: this place
decisions.reason: Balanced follows Isaiah 36:10 except for "this place" (m1), which needs "to ruin it" after it.

decisions.choice: without the permission of the LORD
decisions.reason: Readable explains "without the LORD" as acting without his permission, as in Isaiah 36:10.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶלְיָקִ֣ים בֶּן־חִ֠לְקִיָּהוּ וְשֶׁבְנָ֨ה וְיוֹאָ֜ח אֶל־רַב־שָׁקֵ֗ה דַּבֶּר־נָ֤א אֶל־עֲבָדֶ֨יךָ֙ אֲרָמִ֔ית כִּ֥י שֹׁמְעִ֖ים אֲנָ֑חְנוּ וְאַל־תְּדַבֵּ֤ר עִמָּ֨נוּ֙ יְהוּדִ֔ית בְּאָזְנֵ֣י הָעָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֖ר עַל־הַחֹמָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said Eliakim son of Hilkiah and Shebna and Joah to [the] Rabshakeh, speak please to your servants Aramaic, for understanding [are] we, and do not speak with us Judean in the ears of the people who [are] on the wall.
pieces: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah said to the chief officer, "We beg you, use Aramaic when you talk with your servants, because we know it. Do not talk with us in the language of Judah while the people on the wall are listening."

L.26: And Eliakim son of Hilkiah and Shebna and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, "Speak, please, to your servants [in] Aramaic, for we understand [it]; and do not speak with us [in] Judean in the ears of the people who [are] on the wall."

R.26: Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah said to the Assyrian commander, "Please speak to us in Aramaic. We understand it. Do not speak to us in Hebrew, the language of Judah. The people on the city wall are listening."

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:11
decisions.reason: Kings adds "son of Hilkiah" after Eliakim's name and has "with us" where Isaiah has "to us". The rest is the same.

decisions.choice: Aramaic: the shared language of diplomacy
decisions.reason: Aramaic was spoken across Syria and used throughout the Assyrian empire for letters and treaties. Judah's officials knew it; ordinary people in Jerusalem did not.

decisions.choice: Judean: the language of Judah, Hebrew
decisions.reason: The word names the Hebrew spoken in Judah (Nehemiah 13:24). The officials want the talks kept from the soldiers and people listening on the wall, who would understand every threat.

decisions.choice: your servants: a polite way of saying "us"
decisions.reason: Speaking of oneself as the other's servant was a courteous form of address (Genesis 18:3).

decisions.choice: us ... Hebrew, the language of Judah
decisions.reason: Readable says "us" for the polite "your servants" and gives the language its familiar name, as in Isaiah 36:11.

decisions.choice: the language of Judah
decisions.reason: Balanced explains the word as the language of Judah, since "Judean" alone is not a familiar language name.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶ֜ם רַב־שָׁקֵ֗ה הַעַ֨ל אֲדֹנֶ֤יךָ וְאֵלֶ֨יךָ֙ שְׁלָחַ֣נִי אֲדֹנִ֔י לְדַבֵּ֖ר אֶת־הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה הֲלֹ֣א עַל־הָאֲנָשִׁ֗ים הַיֹּֽשְׁבִים֙ עַל־הַ֣חֹמָ֔ה לֶאֱכֹ֣ל אֶתצוֹאָתָ֗ם וְלִשְׁתּ֛וֹת אֶת־מימֵ֥י רַגְלֵיהֶ֖םעִמָּכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And said to them [the] Rabshakeh, [is it] to your master and to you [that] has sent me my master to speak the words the these? [Is it] not to the men sitting on the wall, to eat their excrement and to drink the water of their feet with you?
pieces: But the chief officer replied to them, "Did my master send me to speak these words just to you and your master? No, they are for the men who sit on the wall, who are going to eat their own dung and drink their own urine along with you!"

L.27: But the Rabshakeh said to them, "[Is it] to your master and to you [that] my master has sent me to speak these words? [Is it] not to the men who sit on the wall, to eat their own excrement and to drink the water of their feet with you?"

R.27: But the Assyrian commander said to them, "My master did not send me to say these things only to you and your master. He sent me to speak to the men sitting on the wall too. When we surround the city, they will have to eat their own waste and drink their own urine, just like you."

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:12
decisions.reason: Kings adds "to them" after "said"; otherwise the verse is the same as Isaiah 36:12.

decisions.choice: their excrement ... the water of their feet: the words read aloud
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text have two blunter words for dung and urine. The Masoretic reading tradition (the qere) replaces them, when read aloud, with the milder "their excrement" and "the water of their feet". The meaning is the same; only the coarseness differs. Isaiah 36:12 has the same pair of readings.

decisions.choice: the water of their feet: urine
decisions.reason: A polite way of naming urine; "feet" is used for the lower body.

decisions.choice: to eat and drink with you: the hunger of a long siege
decisions.reason: The threat is that a siege will bring the city to such hunger and thirst that people are driven to eat and drink filth (compare 6:25). The men on the wall will share that fate with their leaders.

decisions.choice: When we surround the city
decisions.reason: Readable states that the threat is about a siege, which the Hebrew leaves the hearers to supply, as in Isaiah 36:12.

records.source: וַֽיַּעֲמֹד֙ רַב־שָׁקֵ֔ה וַיִּקְרָ֥א בְקוֹל־גָּד֖וֹל יְהוּדִ֑ית וַיְדַבֵּ֣ר וַיֹּ֔אמֶר שִׁמְע֛וּ דְּבַר־הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ הַגָּד֖וֹל מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃
records.gloss: And stood [the] Rabshakeh and called with a voice great [in] Judean, and spoke and said, hear [the] word of the king the great, [the] king of Assyria.
pieces: Then the chief officer stood and shouted in the language of Judah: "Listen to the word of the great king, the king of Assyria!

L.28: And the Rabshakeh stood and called out with a loud voice [in] Judean, and spoke and said, "Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria!

R.28: Then the Assyrian commander stood and shouted loudly in Hebrew, "Listen to what the great king, the king of Assyria, says!

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:13
decisions.reason: Kings adds "and spoke" before "and said", and has "the word" where Isaiah has "the words". The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: stood and called out in Judean: he does the opposite of what was asked
decisions.reason: Instead of moving to Aramaic, the officer takes his stand and shouts in the people's own language, now speaking past the officials to the people on the wall. His speech runs to the end of verse 35.

decisions.choice: Hebrew
decisions.reason: Readable gives the language of Judah its familiar name, as in verse 26.

decisions.choice: shouted ...:
decisions.reason: Balanced folds "called out ... and spoke and said" into one verb, as Isaiah 36:13 does with "called out ... and said".

records.source: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אַל־יַשִּׁ֥יא לָכֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּי־לֹ֣א יוּכַ֔ל לְהַצִּ֥יל אֶתְכֶ֖ם מִיָּדֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Thus says the king, let not deceive you Hezekiah, for not he will be able to deliver you from his hand.
pieces: The king says this: 'Do not let Hezekiah fool you. He has no power to rescue you from the king's hand.

L.29: Thus says the king: 'Let not Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you from his hand.

R.29: This is what the king says: 'Do not let Hezekiah trick you. He cannot save you from me.

decisions.choice: from his hand: not in Isaiah 36:14
decisions.reason: Isaiah 36:14 ends "to deliver you"; Kings adds "from his hand". The king of Assyria speaks of himself as "he": Hezekiah cannot rescue them from the king's power.

decisions.choice: deliver: rescue from an enemy's power
decisions.reason: The verb "deliver" is the key word of verses 29-35, used nine times: Hezekiah cannot deliver, Yahweh will not, and no god has. Chapter 19 shows who can (19:34-35).

decisions.choice: rescue / save
decisions.reason: Balanced says "rescue" and Readable "save" for the verb "deliver" all through verses 29-35, as Isaiah 36 does, so the repeated word stays repeated.

decisions.choice: the king's hand (Balanced); me (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "the king's" so that "his" is not taken to mean Hezekiah; Readable says "me", since the words are the king's own.

records.source: וְאַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְכֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵאמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖נוּ יְהוָ֑ה וְלֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ אֶת־הָעִ֣יר הַזֹּ֔את בְּיַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃
records.gloss: And let not make you trust Hezekiah in Yahweh, saying, surely will deliver us Yahweh, and not will be given the city the this into [the] hand of [the] king of Assyria.
pieces: And do not let Hezekiah lead you to rely on {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} when he tells you, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is sure to rescue us. The king of Assyria will never be given this city."'

L.30: And let not Hezekiah make you trust in {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, saying, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will surely deliver us, and this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria."'

R.30: Do not let him talk you into trusting {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. He says, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will surely save us. The king of Assyria will not be allowed to capture this city."'

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:15
decisions.reason: Kings joins the two halves of Hezekiah's words with "and"; otherwise the verse is the same as Isaiah 36:15.

decisions.choice: make you trust: cause you to rely
decisions.reason: The verb is the causing form of "trust", the word that runs through the speech (verse 19). The officer admits that Hezekiah is calling the people to trust Yahweh, as verse 5 says he did himself.

decisions.choice: this city will not be given: the promise Yahweh keeps
decisions.reason: The officer quotes Hezekiah's confidence to mock it. Yahweh's answer in 19:32-34 is that he will defend this city.

decisions.choice: will not be allowed to capture
decisions.reason: Readable puts "given into the hand of" as being allowed to capture, as in Isaiah 36:15.

records.source: אַֽל־תִּשְׁמְע֖וּ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֜ר מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֗וּר עֲשֽׂוּ־אִתִּ֤י בְרָכָה֙ וּצְא֣וּ אֵלַ֔י וְאִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנוֹ֙ וְאִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵֽנָת֔וֹ וּשְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵֽי־בוֹרֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Do not listen to Hezekiah, for thus says [the] king of Assyria, make with me a blessing and come out to me, and eat each his vine and each his fig tree, and drink each [the] water of his cistern,
pieces: Do not listen to Hezekiah. The king of Assyria says this: 'Come to terms with me and surrender to me. Then everyone may eat from their own vine and their own fig tree and drink water from their own cistern,

L.31: Do not listen to Hezekiah, for thus says the king of Assyria: 'Make a blessing with me and come out to me, and eat each [from] his vine and each [from] his fig tree, and drink each the water of his cistern,

R.31: Do not listen to Hezekiah. The king of Assyria says this: 'Make peace with me. Come out of the city and give yourselves up to me. Then each of you can eat grapes from your own vine and figs from your own fig tree. You can drink water from your own well.

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:16
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as Isaiah 36:16, word for word.

decisions.choice: make a blessing with me: make peace, come to terms
decisions.reason: "Blessing" here is a peace agreement, perhaps sealed with a gift; the word can mean a gift (1 Samuel 25:27; 2 Kings 5:15).

decisions.choice: come out to me: surrender
decisions.reason: To come out to a besieging king meant to open the gates and give up (1 Samuel 11:3; Jeremiah 38:17).

decisions.choice: each his vine and fig tree: a picture of peace
decisions.reason: To enjoy one's own vine and fig tree describes peace and safety, as in Solomon's days (1 Kings 5:5; Micah 4:4). The Assyrian king offers what only Yahweh truly gives.

decisions.choice: well
decisions.reason: Readable says "well" for a cistern, a pit cut in rock to store rainwater, as in Isaiah 36:16.

records.gloss: until I come and take you to a land like your land, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive tree[s] of oil and honey, and live and not die. And do not listen to Hezekiah, for he misleads you, saying, Yahweh will deliver us.
pieces: until I come to move you to a country like your own, a country of grain and fresh wine, of bread and vineyards, of olive oil and honey. Then you will live and not die. Do not listen to Hezekiah, for he is leading you astray when he says, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will rescue us."

L.32: until I come and take you to a land like your land, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees [for] oil, and honey, and live and do not die. And do not listen to Hezekiah, for he misleads you, saying, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will deliver us."

R.32: You can do this until I come and take you away to another country. It will be like your own country. It will have plenty of grain and wine, bread and vineyards, olive oil and honey. Choose to live, not to die! Do not listen to Hezekiah. He is fooling you when he says, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will save us."

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:17-18
decisions.reason: The first part matches Isaiah 36:17. Kings goes on with words Isaiah does not have: "a land of olive oil and honey, and live and do not die". Then where Isaiah 36:18 has "lest Hezekiah mislead you", Kings has "do not listen to Hezekiah, for he misleads you". The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: a land of olive oil and honey: the words used of the promised land
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 8:8 describes the land Yahweh was giving Israel as "a land of olive oil and honey". The Assyrian king promises a new land in the same words, as if he could give what Yahweh gave.

decisions.choice: take you to a land: deportation
decisions.reason: Assyria moved conquered peoples from their homelands to other parts of the empire, as it had done with Israel after Samaria fell (17:6, 24; verse 11). The promise of a good land describes exile.

decisions.choice: live and do not die: the result of surrendering
decisions.reason: The two commands state what will follow if they come out: they will stay alive. They echo Moses' call to "choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19), now turned to the Assyrian king's ends.

decisions.choice: Then you will live and not die
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the commands as the result they promise, which suits the offer.

decisions.choice: You can do this until ...
decisions.reason: Readable begins a new sentence and repeats what the people may do until the king comes, as in Isaiah 36:17.

records.source: הַהַצֵּ֥ל הִצִּ֛ילוּ אֱלֹהֵ֥י הַגּוֹיִ֖ם אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־אַרְצ֑וֹ מִיַּ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃
records.gloss: Have indeed delivered the gods of the nations each his land from [the] hand of [the] king of Assyria?
pieces: Did any of the gods of the nations ever rescue its own land from the hand of the king of Assyria?

L.33: Have the gods of the nations really delivered, each his land, from the hand of the king of Assyria?

R.33: Has the god of any other nation ever saved its country from the king of Assyria?

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:18
decisions.reason: Kings strengthens the verb with a repeated form, "have they really delivered", which Isaiah 36:18 does not have. The question is the same.

decisions.choice: the gods of the nations: Yahweh counted as one god among many
decisions.reason: The officer sets Yahweh alongside the gods of conquered peoples. Hezekiah answers this in his prayer: those gods were "not gods" but the work of human hands, and Yahweh alone is God (19:17-19).

decisions.choice: ever
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable carry the strengthened verb with "ever".

records.gloss: Where [are the] gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where [are the] gods of Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivvah? That they have delivered Samaria from my hand?
pieces: Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did they rescue Samaria from my hand?

L.34: Where [are] the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where [are] the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?

R.34: What happened to the gods of the cities of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did any god save the city of Samaria from me?

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:19
decisions.reason: Kings adds Hena and Ivvah to the list, and its last question begins with a word usually meaning "that" or "indeed" where Isaiah has "and". Some ancient Greek copies add "Where are the gods of the land of Samaria?" before it, which may show how early readers understood the question.

decisions.choice: Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, Ivvah: places Assyria had conquered
decisions.reason: Hamath and Arpad were cities of Syria taken by Assyria in the years before (Isaiah 10:9). People from Sepharvaim and Avva were settled in Samaria after its fall (17:24, 31); Ivvah may be the same place as Avva. Where Hena lay is not known.

decisions.choice: have they delivered Samaria: a question expecting the answer no
decisions.reason: The gods of Samaria, or any gods at all, did not save Samaria from Assyria. Samaria worshiped Yahweh in name and also other gods, and was not spared (verses 9-12; 17:7-18).

decisions.choice: Did any god save
decisions.reason: Readable makes the subject of the question clear, as in Isaiah 36:19.

records.source: מִ֚י בְּכָל־אֱלֹהֵ֣י הָֽאֲרָצ֔וֹת אֲשֶׁר־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־אַרְצָ֖ם מִיָּדִ֑י כִּי־יַצִּ֧יל יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם מִיָּדִֽי׃
records.gloss: Who among all [the] gods of the lands [are those] who have delivered their land from my hand, that should deliver Yahweh Jerusalem from my hand?
pieces: Among all the gods of the lands, which ones have rescued their land from my hand, that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} should rescue Jerusalem from me?'"

L.35: Who among all the gods of the lands [are those] who have delivered their land from my hand, that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} should deliver Jerusalem from my hand?'"

R.35: None of the gods of these countries has saved its land from me. So how could {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} save Jerusalem from me?'"

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:20
decisions.reason: Isaiah has "these lands"; Kings has "the lands". The question is the same.

decisions.choice: that Yahweh should deliver Jerusalem: the boast Yahweh answers
decisions.reason: This is the high point of the speech: Yahweh is just another god who will fail. Yahweh calls this mocking an insult to the Holy One of Israel (19:22), and that night he delivers the city (19:35).

decisions.choice: None of the gods ... has saved ... So how could ...
decisions.reason: Readable turns the rhetorical question into the statement it implies, as in Isaiah 36:20; "these countries" means the lands just named.

records.gloss: And kept silent the people and not answered him a word, for [the] command of the king it [was], saying, not you shall answer him.
pieces: The people stayed silent and did not say a word in reply, for the king had given an order: "Do not answer him."

L.36: And the people kept silent and did not answer him a word, for the king's command was, "Do not answer him."

R.36: But the people stayed silent. No one answered him, because King Hezekiah had commanded, "Do not answer him."

decisions.choice: the people kept silent: the parallel in Isaiah 36:21
decisions.reason: Isaiah 36:21 says only "they kept silent"; Kings names "the people", those on the wall who heard the speech. The three officials kept silent as well, as the king had commanded.

decisions.choice: the king's command: silence as trust
decisions.reason: The people obey their king rather than the voice from outside the wall. They leave the answer to Yahweh, to whom Hezekiah turns in the next chapter (19:1-4, 14-19).

decisions.choice: King Hezekiah
decisions.reason: Readable names which king gave the order.

L.37: And Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who [was] over the house, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder came to Hezekiah [with] torn clothes, and they told him the words of the Rabshakeh.

decisions.choice: the parallel in Isaiah 36:22
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as Isaiah 36:22, word for word, apart from the spelling of two names.

decisions.choice: torn clothes: a sign of grief and alarm
decisions.reason: Tearing one's clothes showed deep distress (Genesis 37:29). Hezekiah does the same when he hears their report (19:1).

decisions.choice: to show their grief
decisions.reason: Readable explains why they tore their clothes.
